results.title: Unequal by age and household type: income inequality and ...
results.content: The methodological approach - a decomposition of income inequality (“a priori approach”) based on household-level rather than individual-level data - underscores the household’s role in mitigating the economic vulnerability of the elderly, a demographic group experiencing unprecedented growth in CEE states. When multi-generational households may mitigate the economic impact of aging through shared support systems, i.e., family-children benefits, buffering against inequality, the single-person households became more polarized due to increased reliance on single incomes or uneven pension incomes within couples. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of income disparities across age groups and household types and their economic impacts on income distribution, demonstrating the critical role of age and household type in driving income inequality across CEE states and addressing the links between population aging and income inequalities. However, differences in how age and household type affect income inequalities between liberal and corporatist states underscore the critical role of welfare state classifications, even in the group of the post-socialist CEE states with the historical similarities of systemic transformation after the demise of the communist rule (Cook & Inglot, 2021).

results.title: The demographic divide: inequalities in ageing across the European ...
results.content: The European Union is projected to enter a period of population decline after 2026, with implications for economic development and labour markets, though these will vary because of different trends in different EU countries. Net migration in these countries is projected to be significantly higher than in Eastern countries, and natural population growth significantly less negative (see the appendix for details per EU country). **Figure 7: EU country groups, changes in natural population, net migration and total population (average annual change/1,000 residents), different scenarios, 2023-2050**. Many Eastern countries already have among the oldest workforces in the EU and are projected to face the largest relative declines in working-age populations. To mitigate the decline of working-age populations, governments will also have to focus on increasing labour-force participation rates among underrepresented groups such as women – gender gaps in labour-force participation are particularly pronounced in Eastern EU countries (Gotti *et al*, 2024).
